title: [Perf][SM90] Score only candidate blocks in the DSv4.1 decode indexer
body:
## Overview

Add a Triton candidate-only decode scoring path for DeepSeek V4.1 on SM90,
reading FP8 K directly from the paged indexer cache instead of scoring the
full context and masking it afterwards.

Related to #61830. This is a separate implementation from the gather-based
prototype in draft #62000: it avoids the intermediate candidate-K buffer.
The flag is off by default (`VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE=1` to enable).

## Claims

- On H20 TP8 with ~1M input tokens, the evalscope A/B below measured a
  **9.6–23.8% reduction in mean ITL** across concurrency 1/2/4/8.
- Consumer logits use 16,384 candidate columns instead of the full compressed
  context. The candidate-source layers, pre-candidate layers and prefill path
  are unchanged.
- Path selection uses configuration checks, not capture-time context lengths.
  Live lengths and page tables remain device inputs during CUDA graph replay.

These results cover the measured long-context workload, not a general
no-regression claim. Accuracy and shorter-workload checks are still pending.

## Validation

### Environment

- Machine: 8x NVIDIA H20 96GB, TP8; driver 535.161.08, CUDA 13.0
- Software: torch 2.14.0+cu130, triton 3.8.0, deep_gemm 2.8.1, vLLM at this
  PR's commit
- Server: `--tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 1048576 --max-num-seqs 16
  --enable-prefix-caching`, speculative decoding with
  `num_speculative_tokens=5`. The A/B runs differ only in
  `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE` (0 vs 1)

### Test guards

```bash
pytest -q tests/kernels/attention/test_candidate_paged_logits.py
```

The tests cover:

- **Scores and selection:** candidate logits against an FP32 reference
  (`rtol=2e-2`, `atol=1e-2`), plus selected-set comparisons for `persistent`
  and `auto` top-k. This is kernel-level coverage, not model accuracy.
- **Cache layout:** page gaps of 0/64/260 bytes with block sizes 16/64;
  invalid cache entry widths are rejected.
- **Bounds:** empty contexts, padded/out-of-range candidate blocks, and
  per-row causal limits during speculative decoding.
- **CUDA graphs:** capture on a short context, replay with changed lengths
  and page tables, then compare against eager execution.
- **Gating and workspace:** default-off behavior, rejected configurations,
  and reuse of the reserved workspace without growth during capture.
- **Performance smoke test:** an effective-bandwidth threshold over the
  candidate path, intended to catch severe regressions, not to measure
  isolated HBM bandwidth.

The current L4 attention CI job skips the SM90 GPU cases. A saved H20 pytest
report for the submitted revision is still needed; the coverage above does
not imply those cases passed in CI.

### End-to-end A/B (1M context)

I ran both configurations on the same commit with the same client arguments.
There is one run per configuration, with 2/4/8/16 measured requests at
concurrency 1/2/4/8 respectively. Set `MODEL` to the served model name and
`TOKENIZER_PATH` to the matching local checkpoint:

```bash
evalscope perf \
  --model "$MODEL" --api openai --stream --api-key EMPTY \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8021/v1/chat/completions \
  --dataset random --tokenizer-path "$TOKENIZER_PATH" \
  --prefix-length 1028976 --min-prompt-length 1024 --max-prompt-length 1024 \
  --number 2 4 8 16 --parallel 1 2 4 8 --warmup-num 1 \
  --max-tokens 16384 --temperature 0.7 --top-p 0.95 --seed 42 \
  --extra-args '{"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}, "ignore_eos": true}'
```

The logs report 1,029,974 input tokens and 16,384 output tokens per request.
The configured prefix length is 1,028,976; input counts above are the measured
counts after prompt construction, not a sum of the CLI length arguments.
The tables report zero cached prompt tokens, but that alone does not verify
server-side prefix-cache hits, especially with this shared-prefix workload.

| Conc. | ITL avg (ms) dense -> cand | ITL p50 (ms) dense -> cand | ITL p90 (ms) dense -> cand |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 12.27 -> 11.09 (**-9.6%**) | 12.28 -> 11.14 (-9.3%) | 12.73 -> 11.73 (-7.9%) |
| 2 | 15.85 -> 13.68 (**-13.7%**) | 16.11 -> 13.50 (-16.2%) | 16.50 -> 14.37 (-12.9%) |
| 4 | 23.01 -> 18.31 (**-20.4%**) | 23.11 -> 18.81 (-18.6%) | 23.64 -> 19.47 (-17.6%) |
| 8 | 35.14 -> 26.78 (**-23.8%**) | 37.19 -> 27.05 (-27.3%) | 38.04 -> 27.88 (-26.7%) |

Secondary metrics from the same runs:

| Conc. | Decode toks/s | Spec. accept dense -> cand | TTFT avg (ms) dense -> cand |
| ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 1 | +20.6% | 81.6% -> 83.0% | 4879.9 -> 4631.7 (-5.1%) |
| 2 | +30.1% | 81.7% -> 83.5% | 5822.9 -> 6107.6 (+4.9%) |
| 4 | +13.3% | 82.0% -> 80.8% | 8322.4 -> 7800.7 (-6.3%) |
| 8 | +21.5% | 81.8% -> 80.8% | 11900.4 -> 11179.7 (-6.1%) |

I use ITL as the main latency metric here, with TPOT and throughput as
supporting results. Under speculative decoding, streamed chunks can contain
multiple tokens: client ITL is not necessarily one GPU iteration, nor is it
independent of acceptance, scheduling or buffering. TPOT remains a valid
user-facing metric, but neither metric alone isolates the kernel change.

This is one A/B pair, not a confidence-interval result. Many intervals within
the same requests do not replace independent runs. At concurrency 4, overall
completion throughput was 827.33 -> 814.72 tok/s (-1.5%) despite lower ITL,
so this is not a throughput win at every concurrency.

I also ran an earlier TP4 test at 200K context. It showed a much smaller ITL
change; the TP8 evalscope run and trace below are the main evidence here.

### Kernel-level trace

The measurement record uses **PyTorch Profiler**, with 100 decode iterations
at ~1M context and client concurrency 12. On rank 0:

| Observation | Dense | Candidate-only |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Mean decode rows/step | 55.2 | 44.3 |
| Scoring time/call | 2027.0 us | 56.4 us |
| Candidate expansion + remap/call | — | 8.2 + 1.8 us |
| Candidate mask + flags, total | 68.10 ms | absent |
| Cooperative top-k time/call | 221.1 us | 94.2 us |

The dense scoring bucket groups the candidate source and four consumers;
the new scoring kernel runs only for the four consumers. All eight ranks
show the new kernel and no consumer mask kernel (400 scoring calls per rank).
This confirms that serving actually exercises the new path.

The batches differ, so these are attribution measurements, not a matched-load
speedup. Even dividing by row count does not fully remove differences in
occupancy and batch composition. End-to-end latency comes from evalscope,
not the profiler's summed CUDA time.

### Accuracy

Model-level accuracy results are pending. I'll compare the flag on and off
with lm-eval and add the results here before merge. Kernel tests alone do not
establish model accuracy. Other SM90 GPUs have not been tested.

## Details

The path prepares per-row candidate blocks and causal bounds, reads candidate
K directly through the page table, scores into a compact buffer, runs the
existing top-k, and remaps the selected columns to request-local positions.
It reuses candidate preparation and remapping from vLLM's SM100 sparse path.
FP8 dot products use FP32 accumulation; invalid columns are masked and valid
column counts are passed to top-k.

For the tested model, `index_head_dim=128`, `index_n_heads=32`,
`candidate_topk_blocks=2048`, `candidate_block_size=8`, and `index_topk=512`.
The compact FP32 logits buffer is `[rows, 16384]` (1.5 MiB at 24 rows).
With five speculative tokens, six decode rows represent one fully populated
request in the kernel input; this is not necessarily the client's concurrent
request count because scheduling and graph padding can change the batch.

The path requires SM90, an FP8 indexer cache, no DCP/PCP, and supported
candidate geometry. When disabled or rejected by the availability check, the
existing dispatch remains in use; existing unsupported combinations may still
raise errors. The gate has no batch-size or context-length profitability
threshold. Avoiding a K copy does not remove preparation, sorting, top-k and
remapping costs, so short-context performance still needs checking.

## What's next

- **Accuracy:** compare lm-eval results with the flag off and on.
- **Performance outside 1M:** benchmark shorter contexts, small batches and
  smaller real datasets to check for latency or throughput regressions.
- **Kernel work:** try a CUDA/CUTLASS implementation and compare it with
  Triton. I'll profile scoring, candidate preparation and top-k before
  deciding which part to optimize; there is no measured speedup for this yet.

I'd appreciate feedback on the implementation while I finish the accuracy and
short-workload checks. Those results still need to be confirmed before merge.
Prefill optimization is outside this PR.

title: [Perf][Attention] Candidate-only FP8 indexer decode scoring on SM90
body:
> **Status: draft.** Opened early to get direction feedback before investing in
> the long-term version. The optimization itself works and is measured; the
> path-selection policy is deliberately provisional and will be reworked (see
> [Roadmap](#roadmap)). Comments on the approach are more useful than comments
> on the gating details, which are expected to change.

## Overview

On SM90 the DSv4.1 candidate-consuming indexers have no paged sparse scoring
kernel, so they score the entire compressed context per decode row and then
mask down to the candidate blocks. This adds an opt-in path that gathers the
candidate K from the paged FP8 indexer cache and scores only the candidates.
Implements the alternative-A direction of #61830.

Not a duplicate: #57858 and #57859 implement candidate-only scoring for ROCm
(gfx950); this is the SM90/CUDA counterpart called for in #61830.

## Claims

Claiming only what is measured at this stage:

- At ~1M context, 9 concurrent requests on 8x H20 (TP8): the four
  candidate-consuming indexer layers drop from **9.57 ms to 3.05 ms** per step,
  and per-step time from **39.04 ms to 31.53 ms** (profiler-derived).
- Selected top-k sets are equivalent to the existing dense score-then-mask
  path.
- Default behaviour is unchanged: the feature is off by default, and
  unsupported shapes or platforms fall back to dense rather than failing.
- Known cost: a single-request step is about **11.6% slower** than dense, since
  the candidate path carries a per-step fixed cost. The provisional workload
  gates exist to avoid that region until a better policy lands.

## Validation

Setup: 8x H20, TP8, DSv4.1, `num_speculative_tokens=5`, ~1M token context.
With `1 + 5 = 6` tokens per request the SM90 paged kernel takes the flatten
path, so one active request contributes roughly 6 decode rows.

**Kernel / unit**

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_candidate_gather_cudagraph.py
pytest tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py
```

- `test_candidate_gather_cudagraph.py` (new): gather + scoring + remap under
  CUDA graph capture and replay.
- `test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py` (extended): dense vs. candidate-only
  equivalence of the selected top-k set.

**Equivalence**

With `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_FORCE=1`, the selected top-k index set matches
the dense path on identical inputs. Note that #61830's alternative-A hoped for
bit-identical results; this verifies set equivalence instead, since the
gather-then-score path uses a different scoring kernel and top-k tie-breaking
can differ (documented in the module docstring).

**Server-level**

Real `vllm serve` at ~1M context, torch profiler traces collected with the
feature off and on:

| Configuration | Per step | Four consumer indexer layers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dense (feature off) | 39.04 ms | 9.57 ms |
| Candidate-only (feature on) | 31.53 ms | 3.05 ms |

at 9 concurrent requests (~54 decode rows).

To reproduce, enable on an SM90 FP8-cache deployment:

```bash
export VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_DECODE=1
export VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_ROWS=16
```

**Validation still in progress** — explicit about what the numbers above do
*not* yet cover, and queued in this order:

1. A profiler-free end-to-end throughput/latency A/B (current timings are
   profiler-derived).
2. Model-level accuracy evaluation plus an independent numerical reference
   (correctness evidence so far is top-k set equivalence against vLLM's own
   dense path).
3. Cross-hardware validation on SM90 parts other than H20 — the reason no
   crossover constant is hardcoded.

I will keep appending results to this PR as they come in.

## Details

**Why the dense path is wasteful here.** The candidate-consuming indexers are
handed a small, fixed-width candidate set, but SM90 lacks a paged sparse
scoring kernel, so they score the whole context and discard everything outside
the candidate blocks. The discarded work grows linearly with context length
(~98% of the scoring work at 1M context, per #61830).

**What the new path does.**

1. Gather each candidate block's K from the paged FP8 indexer cache into a
   compact per-row buffer.
2. Score only the gathered candidates with the existing non-paged FP8 scoring
   kernel.
3. Remap the selected columns back to request-local token positions, so the
   output is identical in meaning to the dense path.

**Scope kept narrow on purpose.** Only the candidate-consuming indexers take
the new path; the candidate-source and pre-candidate indexers stay dense, as
they have no candidate set to exploit. Restricted to SM90 with an FP8 indexer
cache and no context parallelism — SM100 already has native sparse kernels,
and all other platforms keep today's behaviour.

**Tradeoff, and why the current gating is provisional.** Dense cost scales
with `rows x context`, while candidate scoring is dominated by a per-step
fixed cost, so the crossover tracks scanned work relative to the candidate
width rather than context length alone. Since the profitable threshold is
hardware-dependent, this PR does not bake in a device-specific constant and
instead exposes host-side gates (details collapsed below), treating them as a
**stopgap, not the intended final interface**. Defaults impose only
shape-level lower bounds, and the H20 values above are reported as
measurements, not recommended defaults.

**Known structural limitation.** Path selection is host-side per step and is
*not* graph-aware: a fully-captured CUDA graph fixes whichever path was active
at capture time. `FORCE` exists to make that behaviour testable. This is the
main reason the feature ships disabled by default.

<details>
<summary>Workload gates (provisional)</summary>

| Env var | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_DECODE` | `0` | Master switch. |
| `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_ROWS` | `1` | Minimum decode rows in the step (speculative rows included). |
| `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_WORK_RATIO` | `1` | Requires `rows * context >= ratio * candidate_width`. |
| `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_FORCE` | `0` | Validation only: bypass the workload gates. |

</details>

## Roadmap

This PR is a reviewable first increment, not the finished design:

1. **Graph-aware path selection**, so the choice is not frozen by full CUDA
   graph capture. This is the blocker for enabling the feature by default.
2. **Replace the manual env gates** with an automatic, device-independent
   decision (calibration or a cost model), with proper small-batch protection
   instead of a hand-set row threshold.
3. **Longer term**, a native paged sparse scoring kernel for SM90 is the
   cleaner fix than gather-then-score — a much larger change. This PR first
   establishes whether the candidate-only direction is worth it, which the
   numbers above suggest it is.

Happy to run specific concurrency levels, context lengths, or accuracy
benchmarks on request.

title: [Feature]: Candidate-only scoring for DeepSeek-V4.1 indexer consumers on SM90 (H20)
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

> **Scope:** this is a CUDA / SM90 (Hopper) request. ROCm is referenced only as prior art — the bot CC'd ROCm maintainers on keywords, apologies for the noise.

DeepSeek-V4.1's two-level indexer publishes candidate blocks at `candidate_source_layer_id`; later consumer indexers are meant to select their top-k **inside those candidate blocks only**. On SM100 this is implemented with DeepGEMM's sparse MQA-logits kernels (`fp8_fp4_(paged_)sparse_mqa_logits`). On SM90 there is no equivalent, so the consumers fall back to dense scoring over the full context followed by a mask.

vLLM currently implements candidate-consuming indexers in one of two ways:

1. **SM100** — `fp8_fp4_sparse_mqa_logits` / `fp8_fp4_paged_sparse_mqa_logits` via `DeepseekV41SparseIndexerBackend`. Opt-in through `AttentionConfig.indexer_sparse_logits` and hard-gated on SM100-class hardware (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_indexer.py`, the `is_device_capability_family(100)` check), the MXFP4 indexer cache, DeepGEMM >= 2.8, and the DeepSelect extension.
2. **ROCm (gfx950)** — candidate-only MQA scorers reading the candidate pool in place, in review as #57858 (prefill) and #57859 (decode).
3. **SM90 (H20)** — neither. The consumers run the full-width `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/sparse_attn_indexer.py` and then mask the scores down to the candidate blocks with `_apply_candidate_mask` (`vllm/model_executor/kernels/attention/dsa/candidate_blocks.py`). The candidate mechanism keeps the semantics but not the compute saving.

Measured on H20 (SM90), TP8, 1M context, decode, FP8 indexer cache, torch profiler:

| Concurrency | Per consumer layer | 4 consumer layers | Share of a step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ~10 | 2.067 ms | 8.28 ms | 20% of 40.75 ms |
| 1 | 196 µs | 0.78 ms | 6% |

Layers 24/28/32/36 each make one full-context `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` call per step. With `candidate_topk_blocks` = 2048 and `candidate_block_size` = 8, the candidate set is 16 384 positions against a 1 048 576-position compressed context — **1.6% of the scored columns** — so roughly 98% of each consumer's scoring work is discarded by the mask. The cost scales linearly with both concurrency and context length.

The requested feature is a CUDA/SM90 way to score only the candidate blocks.

### The MXFP4 coupling blocks SM90 today

`indexer_sparse_logits` cannot be enabled on SM90 at all, and not only because of the GPU-family check. The flag also requires the MXFP4 indexer cache (`sparse_indexer.py`, and again in `models/deepseek_v41/attention.py`), and MXFP4 itself is rejected before that:

```python
# vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py
if use_fp4 and not current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100):
    raise ValueError(
        "indexer_kv_dtype='mxfp4' requires Blackwell datacenter GPUs "
        "(sm_10x, e.g. B200/GB200); sm_120 (consumer Blackwell) and "
        "earlier architectures are not supported."
    )
```

Hopper has no FP4 datapath, so SM90 necessarily runs the FP8 indexer cache (the `auto` default, one float32 scale per token). MXFP4 is an input requirement of the SM100 DeepGEMM kernels, not part of the "score only the candidate blocks" semantics — the ROCm path, for instance, scores the candidate pool with fp32 logits. So enabling candidate-only scoring on SM90 means letting that semantic flag be satisfied by an FP8 implementation.

**Question for maintainers:** should candidate-only scoring on SM90 reuse `indexer_sparse_logits` (relaxing its MXFP4 requirement to a per-platform one), or should it be a separate opt-in with its own builder type? The former keeps one user-facing knob and makes a future SM100 migration a no-op; the latter keeps each platform's preconditions self-contained.

### Alternatives

- **A. Gather + reuse the existing dense kernel (preferred).** Consumers gather their candidate K from the index cache (~2 MB per request) and score the gathered candidate set with the existing dense logits kernel, dropping the mask pass. No new scoring kernel. The scored K set and the query are identical to the dense-then-mask path, so the resulting logits should be bit-identical. A relevant primitive already exists on CUDA: `cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache` (`torch.ops._C_cache_ops`, added in #25931 / #26456) gathers paged indexer K — FP8 values plus the 4-byte scale — into a contiguous workspace, and the prefill path uses it today. It gathers contiguous ranges addressed by `cu_seq_lens`, so it is a starting point rather than a drop-in: candidate-block gathering needs scattered block IDs.
- **B. Native SM90 sparse MQA-logits kernel.** Mirrors the SM100 DeepGEMM semantics with a new SM90 kernel, removing the gather hop. Better ceiling, substantially more implementation and validation cost.
- **C. Two-level selection inside the consumer (HISA-style).** Block-level coarse pass plus a refined pass inside the candidates. Extends the saving to the candidate-source layer and the ratio-2 layers, but changes the scoring semantics and needs accuracy re-validation. Better treated as a follow-up.

Both A and B need a profitability gate, because gathering loads more per key than the dense walk. #57858 measured the crossover at ~1.0–1.5× `span/capacity` and gates at 2.0×. This workload sits at 62.5×, well above the gate, so the gate should not engage in the target scenario.

### Additional context

**Relationship to existing work.** This is the SM90/CUDA counterpart of the ROCm candidate-only scorers. #57858 (prefill) and #57859 (decode, open) implement candidate-only scoring on gfx950, with measured operator speedups of 3.28× (66 rows, ctx 72.1k) and 4.85× (192 rows, ctx 88.5k), and +5.80% end-to-end output throughput with −4.9% p90 TPOT at TP=4, C=32. They list the same consumer layer positions (24/28/32/36). Those PRs are ROCm-only and touch `rocm_aiter_mla_sparse.py`; the CUDA path is unimplemented. This is not a duplicate of them, though all three would touch `candidate_blocks.py`, so ordering matters.

Related, and deliberately out of scope here:

- #56254 wired the DeepGEMM sparse MQA-logits kernels into the V4.1 indexer. Its stated scope is SM100-class GPUs, and it documents "there is no PyTorch fallback anywhere on the path". That is the scoring path this issue proposes to extend to SM90, not to replace.
- #59204 (draft, conflicting) enables the DeepSelect sparse-indexer **top-k** on sm90. That covers the selection stage, not the scoring stage, and does not touch the SM100 gate on the sparse-logits backend.
- #61039 (merged 2026-10-14) made candidate selection length-aware in the decode indexer, removing ~850 µs/step of full-width work at 1M. It explicitly keeps the full-width path as the fallback when DeepSelect is unavailable, so **SM90 does not benefit from it**: `has_deep_select()` is SM100-only, so `select_candidate_blocks` keeps `FULL_WIDTH=True` on Hopper and still runs `torch.topk(2048)` over the full width. SM90 does have usable top-k backends (`cooperative`, `persistent`), so the same length-awareness looks portable. That is a separate, much smaller item (2.1% of a step at conc≈10, but ~6.5% at conc≈1) and would most naturally ride along with the scoring work rather than be filed on its own.
- The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash kernels tracker (#56217) has no discussion of non-SM100 hardware.

**Open items to validate.**

1. Candidate block alignment: `candidate_block_size` = 8 vs the kernel page sizes (32/64).

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Small-head sparse decode on SM90
body: ## Purpose On SM90, FlashMLA's sparse decode tiles query heads by 64 (the WGMMA M dimension). A DeepSeek V4.1 TP8 rank owns only 8 heads (16 at TP4), so it pads them to 64 and spends most of the tensor-core work on padding. This adds a Triton sparse decode kernel that tiles heads by 16 with `tl.dot` (mma.sync), reads the existing packed FP8 MLA cache directly, and recovers parallelism by splitting the key set across programs, merging the partial results with log-sum-exp. **Why it is faster at small batches.** At a few decode tokens per step, FlashMLA launches roughly one CTA per token and each CTA does 64-head work for 8 real heads. This kernel launches `tokens × splits` programs, each doing 16-head work over its share of keys. The best split count depends on both token count and key width: 32 splits at ≤3 tokens fills the GPU, but by 8 tokens 8 splits wins because the merge cost and per-program gather overhead dominate. `_pick_config` encodes this measured table. At larger batches the step becomes gather/dequant-bound rather than MMA-bound, so removing the padding no longer helps and FlashMLA is kept. **Dispatch** (automatic, no flag): SM90, 8 or 16 local heads, decode only, and | Layer key width (SWA + compressed top-k) | Uses this kernel at | Otherwise | | --- | --- | --- | | ≤256 (SWA-only layers) | ≤16 decode tokens per step | FlashMLA | | >256 (compressed layers, `index_topk=512`) | ≤12 decode tokens per step | FlashMLA | The gate is decode tokens per rank per step (≈ batch × (1 + spec tokens)), so the gain is limited to **low-concurrency decode**. It does not depend on context length, since sparse attention reads a fixed number of keys per token. Prefill always uses FlashMLA. **JIT warmup:** both launches register every split config, `HAS_EXTRA` variant and DSpark SWA width with the startup JIT warmup, so no Triton compile happens on the serving path. Related to #48168. **Not a duplicate:** I checked the issue discussion and open PRs for #48168 and for small-head sparse decode; none implements this SM90 decode path. #57673 has since been reworked into an opt-in backend that reuses this PR's decoder (with attribution) but does not add the automatic FlashMLA dispatch. #55866 targets FA4 sparse MQA on *Blackwell*, #51403 targets *ROCm*. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla_sparse.py -k small_head -q python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_dsv41_small_head_decode.py --heads 8 16 --topk 0 64 512 --rounds 3 pre-commit run --all-files ``` End-to-end on 8× H20 (one node), TP8, DSpark K=2, same flags as our production deployment except `--max-model-len 32768`. Both arms ran on the same node and the same image, back-to-back: ```bash vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --ignore-eos --seed 42 \ --max-concurrency {1,2,4,8,16,32} lm_eval --model local-chat-completions --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 \ --apply_chat_template --fewshot_as_multiturn --gen_kwargs temperature=0 ``` ## Test Result ### End-to-end (8× H20, TP8) Median ITL is per decode step; concurrency 1–4 falls inside the gate (≤12 tokens/step with K=2). | Concurrency | Stock median ITL | This PR | Δ ITL | Stock tok/s | This PR tok/s | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 8.99 ms | 8.37 ms | **−6.8%** | 239.6 | 264.4 | | 2 | 10.96 ms | 9.87 ms | **−9.9%** | 365.5 | 400.8 | | 4 | 13.91 ms | 13.11 ms | **−5.7%** | 574.2 | 621.9 | | 8 | 19.52 ms | 19.39 ms | −0.7% | 825.7 | 824.7 | | 16 | 27.48 ms | 27.13 ms | −1.3% | 1135.1 | 1178.9 | | 32 | 41.05 ms | 41.29 ms | +0.6% | 1510.6 | 1522.3 | Throughput also reflects DSpark acceptance length, which varied by run (2.06–2.23 stock vs 2.14–2.31 this PR), so ITL is the cleaner signal. **GSM8K** (full 1319, 5-shot chat, greedy, flexible extract): stock **89.99%** (1187), this PR **89.92%** (1186), stderr ±0.83%. Per question, 19 flip to correct and 20 flip to wrong, consistent with split-K reduction order changing near-tie greedy tokens. ### Operator benchmark (1× H20) 108 configurations (tokens 1–16/24/32 × heads 8/16 × top-k 0/64/512), CUDA graphs, cold-L2 input rotation, median of 3 alternating rounds, CUDA-event timing. Every configuration inside the gate is faster than FlashMLA; none regresses. | Key width | Gate | Speedup inside gate | Outside gate | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | SWA + top-k 0 / 64 | ≤16 tokens | 1.31–2.14x | FlashMLA (kernel would be 1.09–1.40x at 24, ~1.0x at 32) | | SWA + top-k 512 | ≤12 tokens | 1.06–1.42x | FlashMLA (kernel would be 0.90–0.94x at 16–32) | **JIT warmup (8× H20, TP8, DSpark K=2):** with `--jit-monitor-mode warn`, 92 requests at concurrency 1–8 all succeeded with zero small-head kernel compiles after startup; warmup compiles 8 decode + 3 merge variants in 2.3 s on one GPU. **Correctness:** 44 focused tests pass on H20 (FP32 reference and FlashMLA comparisons, 64/128-token pages, 8/16 heads, non-contiguous views, invalid/empty rows, CUDA graph replay, dispatch at the gate boundary). Pre-commit passes. > All GPU results use the vLLM 0.30.0 image with this PR's kernel and dispatch patched in, not an exact-head install. CI results are pending. - [x] Human submitter reviews every changed line and independently runs the tests. - [ ] Full focused suite on an exact-head install, and CI. - [x] Repeat the end-to-end A/B with interleaved runs to tighten the ITL numbers. --- AI assistance: OpenAI Codex and Claude were used to implement, tune, benchmark, and validate this change. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

body:
## Overview

Rework this as an opt-in SM90 backend with centralized selection and separate Triton prefill/decode, as requested in review. DeepSeek V4.1 TP8/TP4 keeps its 8/16 local query heads instead of padding to 64.

## Claims

- Select with `--attention-backend TRITON_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41`; default backend selection is unchanged.
- Eligible verification-query pairs share sparse KV reads. Other decode shapes use the direct Triton decoder.
- H20×8/TP8 output throughput improves 5.4–8.7% in the measured workloads, with lower p95 TTFT and end-to-end latency.

## Validation

Same image and flags, changing only the attention backend. Source and native libraries built from `0c16eee3`; DSpark adaptive/5, Humming 0.1.16/BF16, batch 8192, max 64 sequences, `fp8_ds_mla` and fixed KV budget 22,191,197,696 bytes/GPU.

EvalScope 1.11.1 with a reasoning-field timing fix: 200 streaming requests per point, identical frozen prompts, isolated prefixes, 1024 output tokens with EOS ignored. All requests succeeded; no timed compilation, cache hits or preemptions observed in the included samples.

| Input / concurrency | Output tok/s, FlashMLA → Triton | Change | p95 TTFT | p95 E2E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K / 64 | 1372.8 → 1446.3 | +5.4% | −7.5% | −8.1% |
| 32K / 8 | 399.4 → 434.2 | +8.7% | −8.1% | −10.0% |
| 32K / 32 | 487.4 → 526.9 | +8.1% | −8.7% | −10.8% |
| 32K / 32, repeat | 485.2 → 526.8 | +8.6% | −8.8% | −6.8% |

32K ran Triton→FlashMLA; 8K uses a warmed FlashMLA→Triton rerun because the first candidate sample compiled an auxiliary kernel. Median TTFT was more variable: +1.5% and −29.0% in the two 32K/C32 runs.

84 tests passed (52 CPU, 32 GPU), with zero failures or skips. Coverage includes independent FP32 references, packed/strided KV, large offsets, warmup and mutable CUDA Graph replay. Prefix-growth, named-tool and reasoning-stream checks passed on both backends. Changed-file pre-commit and mypy passed; H100 CI coverage is wired, upstream CI pending.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/test_fewhead_prefill_gate.py \
  tests/kernels/attention/test_fewhead_sparse_prefill.py \
  tests/kernels/test_compressor_kv_cache.py::test_v41_compressor_metadata_maps_tokens_to_their_ring -q
```

Full GSM8K, 16-shot greedy chat, max 1024 tokens: **1281/1319 → 1284/1319**, zero request errors. Three answers changed from correct to wrong and six from wrong to correct; length stops were 1→2. This does not establish output equivalence.

## Details

The direct decoder and packed-KV loader come from [#59418](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59418) by luoyuctl (`eddfa5ed50c1`), with three page-size parameters specialized as `tl.constexpr`. They are isolated in the first commit. This PR adds independent backend integration, native-head prefill and query pairing; it does not add #59418's automatic FlashMLA dispatch. Shared-decoder landing order still needs coordination. Query-union prior art: #55372. Unlike #54592, prefill keeps BF16 queries. Reported gains measure the whole backend, including the shared decoder and DSpark interactions.

Requires SM90, BF16 queries, 512D heads/64D RoPE and packed `fp8_ds_mla` KV. Prefill stays outside FULL CUDA Graphs. The context limit is 1M; measured performance inputs are 8K/32K. TP4 full-model, actual 1M inputs and comprehensive multimodal evaluation are not qualified.

Driver-memory maxima sampled every 60 seconds changed by −2.04 to +1.40 GiB/GPU; the 32K cases used about 1.4 GiB/GPU more. These are sampled values, not exact peaks or a memory-saving claim.

title: [Perf][Marlin] Reduce DS V4.1 Flash MoE padding on SM90
body:
## Purpose

Reduce DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash MXFP4 expert padding on SM90 Marlin. At TP8,
each 288-channel partition uses **320 instead of 384** channels, saving
**7.77 GiB of model-loading memory per H20 GPU** at a fixed KV budget.

The change applies to regular CUDA SM90 Marlin with BF16 activations and
no A8 quantization. Hidden alignment remains 256. This storage-alignment
change is separate from #56744's batched tile selection and #56493's
SM89 block-FP8 tile grouping.

## Test Plan

Rebase validation (`b05a5ca710a9` on `7b942936276d`): the original
patch is unchanged apart from upstream context. **142 MXFP4 tests passed**
on H20 with the prepared native Marlin runtime; changed-file lint and
mypy 3.12 passed. Performance and quality results below retain their
original frozen source versions.

Run from each pinned source tree using the prepared test environment:

```bash
# Both trees: 208 passed each
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 uv run --no-project /study/.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_insert.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py -q
# PR tree: 142 passed
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 uv run --no-project /study/.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/quantization/test_marlin_tile_padding.py \
  tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_weight_loading_padded.py -k mxfp4 -q
```

**558 passed, no skips** in the frozen-source targeted run. The original broader
padding/loading suite passed 281 tests with 13 skips on H20. Tests cover
allocation guards, repack, both expert GEMMs against dequantized weights,
and TP4/TP8 shard loading. The SM90 GPU tests skip on L4 CI workers.
The committed `benchmark_mxfp4_marlin_padding.py` provides a paired
synthetic expert-path benchmark. Pinned Ruff hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

## Test Result

Frozen upstream **`bb5507741155`**, PR **`238e1c21f478`**; identical native
binaries across layouts. H20×8, TP8, BF16, dense emulation, Python API1,
default modalities/Engram, max sequences 64, batch tokens 8192, DSpark 5
adaptive, `fp8_ds_mla`. GPU KV is fixed at 22,191,197,696 bytes/rank;
native SimpleCPUOffloadConnector uses 64 GiB total. The service limit is
1M; the performance inputs below are 8K/32K.

EvalScope 1.11.1, matched random inputs, streaming and exactly 1024 output
tokens. Two complete boots per layout in C→D / D→C order, with separate
priming. Model-loading memory is **51.09 → 43.32 GiB/GPU**.

| Input/concurrency | Round | Baseline tok/s | +PR tok/s | Throughput | E2E p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K/C64 | 1 | 861.71 | 916.19 | +6.3% | -9.1% |
| 8K/C64 | 2 | 850.94 | 916.65 | +7.7% | -7.2% |
| 32K/C4 | 1 | 221.78 | 239.05 | +7.8% | -7.3% |
| 32K/C4 | 2 | 218.73 | 232.51 | +6.3% | -3.2% |

832 measured requests succeeded, plus 384 priming requests. 8K/C4 was
inconsistent, including p95 regressions. C16 and one C4 run overlap JIT
warnings and are excluded from the performance claim above. CPU prefix
hits were zero in these random-input runs; these are PR gains with
offload enabled, not an offload-benefit measurement.

One baseline boot stopped at priming validation after an empty-text
stream had unavailable TTFT. Its 64 completed measurements are retained
separately; the entire boot was repeated with unchanged EvalScope commands
and seeds after correcting only the priming validator.

**Quality:** full GSM8K, three independent boots per layout:

| Layout | Original | Repeat 1 | Repeat 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline | 1277/1319 | 1280/1319 | 1278/1319 |
| +PR | 1275/1319 | 1280/1319 | 1277/1319 |

Zero-shot chat, C16, greedy, thinking=false, max_tokens=1024, request
seed=20260915, server seed=0. Prompt and grading logic were unchanged;
truncations and missing final answers count as incorrect. The differences
remain **−2, 0, −1 answers**. Within-layout repeats change 7–12 final answers;
targeted C1 replays also vary. This does **not** establish quality equivalence
or prove that the negative difference is entirely runtime variation.

An additional 90-case numerical comparison passed the same dequantized
BF16 reference tolerance (`atol=rtol=0.03`) for both padding extents.
Mean relative L2 error was 0.00499137 / 0.00499136. Both layouts also pass
three image, two streamed-tool and 16 controlled KV-retrieval checks.

AI assistance was used; the original patch was reviewed and tested by the submitter.

## Newer-upstream compatibility check (2026-09-22)

Retested the four production-file changes from PR head `b05a5ca710a9`
on upstream `a33b3bac5dad`, using its matching official wheel on H20.
The runtime audit verified 5,147 official wheel files and all four PR
overlay files; native extensions and declared dependency constraints passed.

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 uv run --offline --no-project /study/.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  --confcutdir=/upgrade/validation \
  tests/kernels/quantization/test_marlin_tile_padding.py \
  tests/kernels/test_compressor_kv_cache.py \
  -k 'mxfp4_marlin or dspark_context_kv_matches_query_insert' -q
```

**170 passed, 221 deselected, no skips**: 138 Marlin padding tests and 32
upstream DSpark KV-write tests. The latter are companion upgrade checks,
not additional coverage attributable to this PR. The test source was the
upstream tree plus the PR test changes, with the matching patched wheel.

The newer full-model TP8 service still reports **43.32 GiB/GPU** model-loading
memory with this patch. Its standard serving validation completed 648/648
measured requests successfully (streaming, fixed 1,024 output tokens), and
two basic chat checks passed. These are compatibility and serving checks,
not a new quality evaluation or a clean PR on/off comparison: both compared
deployments include this patch, and the newer deployment also disables CPU
KV offload. The original **7.77 GiB/GPU** reduction and PR-only throughput
measurements remain attributed to the frozen A/B versions above.

title: [Perf][DeepSeek V4.1] Humming indexed MoE GEMM with EP on Hopper, and a named MoE activation format
body:
## Purpose

With `--moe-backend humming` and expert parallelism, Humming runs DeepSeek-V4.1's MXFP4 experts on its grouped GEMM. On Hopper the indexed GEMM is much faster for this model. This PR makes `get_humming_moe_gemm_type()` return `indexed` when all of these hold:

- the experts are MXFP4 with DeepSeek V4 routing;
- `model_type` is `deepseek_v41` or `deepseek_v41_text`;
- the device is CUDA SM90;
- there are no all2all kernels, or the backend is `allgather_reducescatter`.

Without EP, Humming already picks indexed, so nothing changes there. `VLLM_HUMMING_MOE_GEMM_TYPE` still overrides the choice. Since #56997, Humming is the default MXFP4 MoE backend on SM90, so V4.1 with EP on Hopper otherwise runs the grouped GEMM by default; this PR moves that default path to indexed too. The rule applies with BF16 activations and with per-token FP8 activations (`--quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token`).

The MXFP4 MoE method (DeepSeek V4/V4.1, Kimi-K3, plain mxfp4) now runs `quantization_config.moe.activation`:

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash -tp 8 --enable-expert-parallel \
    --moe-backend humming --quantization-config.moe.activation fp8_per_token
```

- Humming takes the named format as a fixed input schema, with its input-schema fallback off.
- Other explicit backends must run the named format, and `auto` keeps only the backends that do. Before, these models ignored the name on every backend. Now a backend that does not run it stops vLLM, on every platform (CUDA, ROCm, XPU, CPU). The DeepSeek V4 MegaMoE backends (`deep_gemm_mega_moe`, `aiter_mega_moe`) build their own experts and do not read the name. On ROCm, the Kimi-K3 AITER path, which skips the backend selector, now refuses a named activation instead of ignoring it. For example, `fp8_per_token` with `flashinfer_trtllm` now stops vLLM instead of running MXFP8. A draft model with its own `speculative_config.moe_backend` inherits the target's `quantization_config`, so the same rule applies to it.
- The startup log prints the format Humming runs: `Humming MoE activations: fp8_per_token (group size 0, scale dtype float32)`. The line appears for every Humming MoE model, gpt-oss included.
- On SM90 Humming, `mxfp8` and `fp8_per_block_dynamic` stop vLLM at startup, before the weights load. Humming has no e8m0 input scales on WGMMA, and humming 0.1.16 rejects fp32 group scales with MXFP4 weights (#60600). Group-wise scales are also 1.2x to 24x slower than per-token in the SM90 Humming GEMM at M >= 256 (numbers in the review reply).
- `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` still works as on main, with no early check: a format Humming cannot run fails while the weights convert, as before. With `--moe-backend humming`, setting it together with `moe.activation` is an error.
- gpt-oss is unchanged. With no name, nothing changes.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_moe.py -k "named_activation or activation_on_sm90 or humming or indexed"
pytest tests/quantization/test_quantization_config_args.py \
    tests/quantization/test_humming_mxfp4_block_fp8.py tests/kernels/moe/test_b12x.py \
    tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py tests/quantization/test_gfx950_moe.py
pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_gfx942_int4.py
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_ocp_mx_moe.py -k unsupported_reasons
```

`test_humming_deepseek_v41_hopper_uses_indexed_gemm_with_ep` calls `get_humming_moe_gemm_type` and checks that V4.1 with EP gets indexed, with and without `allgather_reducescatter`, and that DeepEP, SM100 and DeepSeek V4 keep the grouped GEMM. It does not need the humming package.

`test_deepseek_v4_mxfp4_backend_must_run_named_activation` checks on any GPU that `auto` and `flashinfer_trtllm` refuse `fp8_per_token`, and that `humming` refuses the env JSON plus a name ("not both"). `test_humming_deepseek_v4_activation_on_sm90` checks that SM90 Humming accepts `fp8_per_token` and refuses `mxfp8`. It skips on other GPUs, so in CI it runs only in the optional H100 FP8 MoE kernels job; `kernels-moe-test` runs on L4. The Kimi-K3 AITER refusal has no unit test: it is a short guard, and a test would have to mock the whole K3 path.

## Test Result

Unit tests on one H200: the `test_moe.py` selection above, 41 passed (the SM90 test runs there, not skipped). title: [Perf][DeepSeek V4] Default to block FP8 MoE activations on Hopper with EP
body:
## Overview

Proof of concept: on Hopper with expert parallel, run DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 MXFP4 experts on Humming with block FP8 (group 128) activations by default instead of BF16. Related to #59488 (opt-in `--quantization-config.moe.activation` for the same method), which this would rebase onto.

## Claims

- DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TP4 + EP on H200: +25% decode output throughput (TPOT 25.2 -> 20.0 ms) and +6% prefill-heavy throughput, with GSM8K unchanged.
- Scope: `Mxfp4MoEMethod` with the HUMMING backend, DeepSeek V4 routing (V4 and V4.1), expert parallel, SM90. Everything else keeps the current BF16 default, and `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` still overrides.

## Validation

DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 4x H200, Humming MoE backend (the SM90 default). Baseline is `main` (BF16 activations). The FP8 column was measured with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG='{"a_dtype": "float8e4m3", "input_scale_group_size": 128}'`. That override resolves to the same Humming layer config as this PR's `kFp8Dynamic128Sym` (group 128, `DynamicGroup`, float32 scales on SM90).

| Config | Workload | BF16 (main) | FP8 GS128 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP4 + EP | GSM8K 5-shot (1319 q) | 0.951 | 0.948 | within noise |
| TP4 + EP | decode: 512 in / 1024 out, conc 128 (3 runs) | 4757 / 4911 / 4906 tok/s | 6131 / 6135 / 6128 tok/s | **+25%** |
| TP4 + EP | prefill: 8192 in / 64 out, conc 32 | 28939 tok/s total | 30780 tok/s total | +6.4% |
| TP4 + EP | low concurrency: 2048 in / 512 out, conc 4 | 422.6 tok/s | 421.0 tok/s | -0.4% |
| TP4 (no EP) | GSM8K 5-shot | 0.948 | 0.951 | within noise |
| TP4 (no EP) | decode (1 run) | 5249 tok/s | 4473 tok/s | -15% |
| TP4 (no EP) | prefill | 29873 tok/s total | 30309 tok/s total | +1.5% |
| TP4 (no EP) | low concurrency | 485.9 tok/s | 455.9 tok/s | -6% |

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel --max-model-len 16384
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 --max-concurrency 256
vllm bench serve --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 512 --random-output-len 1024 --num-prompts 512 --max-concurrency 128 --ignore-eos
```

Tests: `pytest tests/quantization/test_humming_mxfp4_block_fp8.py` passes (11). The new test fails without the source change.

## Details

DeepSeek V4 MXFP4 experts go through `Mxfp4MoEMethod`, which passes no activation key. On SM90 the Humming backend then builds its input schema from `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` and defaults to BF16. This PR sets `activation_key = kFp8Dynamic128Sym` in that case. #59815 already plumbs the key into Humming's input schema with fallback disabled. The DeepSeek V4 checkpoint declares block FP8 GS128 with UE8M0 scales for its FP8 layers, so block FP8 matches what the model was built for.

Why only with EP: under EP each rank runs full-size experts (hidden 4096, intermediate 2048), where Humming's FP8 x MXFP4 kernels are faster. Under TP4 the intermediate is split to 512 per rank, and dynamic activation quantization costs more than it saves. Gating on DeepSeek V4 routing keeps other MXFP4 models (Kimi K3, plain mxfp4) unchanged.

Limitations:
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash was not run; it shares the routing and method, so it gets the same default. #59488 reports the indexed GEMM is faster for V4.1 with EP on Hopper, and the FP8 gain should be re-measured on that path.
- Measured on H200 with the default all2all backend. DeepEP v2 and H100/H20 were not measured.
- The FP8 column was measured with the equivalent env override. I could not rerun end to end on this exact build because the shared machine's GPUs were taken.
- Not a duplicate: #59488 adds an opt-in activation format for the same method, and this PR changes the default for one configuration. #53184 fuses SwiGLU with per-token FP8 quantization for W2. #53709 dequantizes experts to block FP8 instead.

title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Split fused_wqa_wkv by token across TP ranks on SM90
body:
## Purpose

Without sequence parallelism, every TP rank computes DeepSeek-V4.1's `fused_wqa_wkv` (5120 → 1280 + 512) for all tokens, so all ranks do the same work. The checkpoint stores this weight as FP8 with UE8M0 block scales, which vLLM runs through its MXFP8 path. On SM90 that path is a W8A16 Marlin GEMM: on H20 it takes 1.79 ms per layer for an 8192-token prefill chunk, 72 ms per chunk over the 40 layers.

This PR splits the projection by token for batches of at least 2048 tokens. Each rank projects its token shard (`sp_shard`), and `sp_all_gather` rebuilds `qr_kv`. The change is confined to `DeepseekV4Attention._fused_wqa_wkv_gemm`:
- `_run_parallel_input_projections` is unchanged, so the multi-stream decision is the same as on main.
- The all-gather is issued on the current stream, right after the GEMM that produces its input.

`_shard_fused_wqa_wkv` in the NVIDIA decoder layer enables the split only when all of the following hold:
- **SM90.** On SM100, `fused_wqa_wkv` runs as a native MXFP8 GEMM, far cheaper than W8A16 Marlin, so the gather would be a much larger share of the cost. I have not measured SM100, and the H20 results below do not carry over to it.
- **No sequence parallelism.** There the hidden states are already sharded, and #57257 splits this projection for that case.
- **No LoRA.** The LoRA wrapper maps every token of the batch.
- **No micro-batching.** Two micro-batches would share the custom all-gather buffer.
- **No batch invariance.** Whether a token takes the split depends on the batch size.
- **The custom all-reduce is enabled and fully connected.** This serves only as a proxy for NVLink between all TP ranks. From 6144 tokens at TP8, the shard exceeds the custom all-gather's 2 MiB limit, so the gather itself runs on NCCL.

TP4 and TP2 take the same gate but were not measured. On Hopper they need pipeline parallelism to hold the checkpoint.

The compressor's `fused_wkv_wgate` and the indexer's `weights_proj` stay replicated, and `_run_parallel_input_projections`, which can run them on separate streams, is unchanged. They appear in only a few layers:
- the compressor in the 4 KV-source layers (2, 8, 14, 20);
- the indexer in the 8 index-source layers, which are those four plus 24, 28, 32 and 36.

At 8192 tokens, splitting them as well would save at most another 457 µs in a KV-source layer (last column of the second table; layer 20's compressor is half as wide). In the four indexer-only layers the projection is only 5120 → 32. This PR saves about 1.45 ms in each of the 40 layers, so it limits the split to this dominant projection.

**Why 2048 tokens.** On H20 the split is faster from 48 tokens (first table below). H100 and H200 have about 6.7 times H20's dense throughput with the same 900 GB/s NVLink, so the replicated GEMM costs much less there while the gather costs the same.

I have no H100 or H200 to measure on, so I scaled the H20 numbers pessimistically:
- a GEMM of 1024 rows or more runs 6.7 times faster than on H20;
- one of 512 rows runs 3.7 times faster, and one of 256 rows or fewer only twice as fast;
- the gather runs no faster.

Under these assumptions the break-even is about 1450 tokens, and 2048 is the next power of two. A measurement on H100 or H200 would confirm or retune it.

**Related work.** I found no upstream PR for the case without sequence parallelism. The fork commit bytedance-iaas/vllm@383776ac20 splits `fused_wqa_wkv` the same way, but behind an environment variable that is off by default, and not when speculative decoding is on.

## Test Plan

**Kernel benchmark.** Setup:
- Hardware: 8× H20 (SM90, 96 GB, NVLink), TP8.
- Software: torch 2.13.0+cu130, NCCL 2.29.7, vLLM nightly `0.30.1rc1.dev85+g8b84e1506` with this diff applied as a Python overlay.
- What it runs: `fused_wqa_wkv` is built as the model builds it, with random weights and the checkpoint's quantization, so SM90 runs Marlin. The second table times `_run_parallel_input_projections` from this branch, which calls `_fused_wqa_wkv_gemm`, with the model's projection shapes and three aux streams.

Timing follows `.agents/skills/kernel-microbenchmark`:
- One CUDA graph per candidate.
- Before every measured replay, an L2 flush (twice the L2 size) and a device-side barrier, both outside the timed interval.
- The time of a replay is the CUPTI span of its kernels. Each sample is the maximum over the 8 ranks, and the tables report the median of 50 samples.
- Candidates alternate within every round, and correctness is checked before timing.

The benchmark script is not part of this PR; I can add it under `benchmarks/kernels/` if that helps.

**Serving.** TP8 without expert parallelism. DSpark uses synthetic acceptance with a mean acceptance length of 3.51, the same distribution in both arms:

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash --revision dba1be0a40aa45a94ad051997016db3960a90277 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --language-model-only --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --max-model-len 262144 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 128 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":false}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"synthetic","synthetic_acceptance_length":3.51,"enable_adaptive_verification":false}'
```

One `vllm bench serve` call per point:

| Point | ISL | OSL | C | N |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8K / 32K / 128K prompt TTFT | 8192 / 32768 / 131072 | 1 | 1 | 5 / 3 / 2 |
| 1K in / 1K out, C1 | 1024 | 1024 | 1 | 6 |
| 1K in / 1K out, C64 | 1024 | 1024 | 64 | 192 |
| 8K in / 1K out, C16 | 8192 | 1024 | 16 | 48 |
| 8K in / 1K out, C64 | 8192 | 1024 | 64 | 128 |

```bash
vllm bench serve --backend openai --endpoint /v1/completions --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len <ISL> --random-output-len <OSL> --random-range-ratio 0 --ignore-eos \
  --max-concurrency <C> --num-prompts <N> --num-warmups <C> --seed 1
```

Each arm ran on a fresh server, in the order this PR (B1), main (A1), main (A2), this PR (B2).

**Accuracy.** Full GSM8K (1,319 questions) through `/v1/chat/completions`, with real DSpark verification (`rejection_sample_method: block`) instead of synthetic acceptance:
- 5-shot multi-turn chat with thinking off (`chat_template_kwargs: {"thinking": false}`);
- temperature 0, seed 123, `max_tokens` 1024, 32 concurrent requests;
- each reply is scored by the number after `####`, or else by its last number.

## Test Result

**`fused_wqa_wkv`, split vs replicated** (µs per call, TP8, every batch size split so the crossover is visible):

| Tokens | Rows per rank | Replicated | Split + all-gather | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 6 | 1 | 14.1 | 23.2 | 0.61x |
| 12 | 2 | 14.6 | 23.1 | 0.63x |
| 24 | 3 | 19.2 | 21.1 | 0.91x |
| 48 | 6 | 25.9 | 20.3 | 1.28x |
| 96 | 12 | 49.6 | 21.5 | 2.31x |
| 384 | 48 | 99.7 | 35.8 | 2.78x |
| 1024 | 128 | 239.4 | 66.8 | 3.58x |
| 2048 | 256 | 458.5 | 99.7 | 4.60x |
| 4096 | 512 | 903.6 | 173.3 | 5.22x |
| 8192 | 1024 | 1794.7 | 346.9 | 5.17x |
| 16384 | 2048 | 3570.8 | 635.4 | 5.62x |

Up to 4096 tokens the gather is the custom all-reduce's all-gather; from 6144 tokens it is NCCL. From 4096 tokens on, the replicated Marlin GEMM runs at 83–84 TFLOPS.

**Input projections of one attention layer, main vs this PR** (µs; only this stage is timed, not the whole layer):

| Tokens | Layer without compressor or indexer (32 layers): main | This PR | Speedup | Layer with compressor and indexer (layers 2, 8, 14): main | This PR | Speedup | If compressor and indexer were also split |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 | 236.7 | 236.5 | same code | 337.6 | 337.7 | same code | 337.5 |
| 1536 | 351.1 | 348.8 | same code | 478.5 | 480.6 | same code | 481.1 |
| 2048 | 458.1 | 99.9 | 4.59x | 660.4 | 301.8 | 2.19x | 198.3 |
| 4096 | 903.0 | 172.7 | 5.23x | 1276.2 | 545.9 | 2.34x | 343.5 |
| 8192 | 1794.2 | 346.0 | 5.19x | 2473.9 | 1028.4 | 2.41x | 571.6 |
| 16384 | 3569.4 | 635.6 | 5.62x | 4902.1 | 1976.6 | 2.48x | 1052.3 |

- **Estimate per 8K prefill chunk:** this stage gets about 1.45 ms faster in every layer, about 58 ms over the 40 layers. The serving results below are the measurement.
- **Correctness:** `qr_kv` differs from the replicated projection by at most 0.031 across two sweeps with different inputs. That is bf16 rounding from Marlin's M-dependent tiling. `kv_score` and `indexer_weights` are bitwise identical to main.

**Serving and accuracy.** The serving numbers are a sanity check with two servers per arm, not a precise measurement. Lower TTFT and higher output throughput are better, and Change compares the means of the two arms.

title: [WIP][Kernel][DSv4.1] Add compensated BF16 mHC prenorm for SM90
body:
## Purpose

Draft a compensated BF16 mHC prenorm primitive for Hopper, adapted from SGLang's `hc_mix_stats_bf16x3` in sgl-project/sglang#39664 and sgl-project/sglang#41251. It splits the FP32 mixing weight into three BF16 components, accumulates their projections separately in FP32, and computes the input squared norm in the same pass.

This initial draft contains a kernel, correctness tests and a comparison benchmark. **Serving dispatch is intentionally not wired yet. No kernel or end-to-end speedup, numerical equivalence, or production-readiness claim is made.** Integration and default selection depend on real SM90 measurements against the current fused mHC path, not only against a standalone GEMM.

## Implementation

- Accept caller-owned prepared weights and output buffers; no allocation or CPU/GPU synchronization in the projection wrapper.
- Write `[splits, tokens, mix]` projection and `[splits, tokens]` squared-norm partials, compatible with the existing prenorm epilogue layout.
- Support split counts 1/4/16, token tiles 32/64/128, empty batches, masked tails, and contiguous offset views. These are tuning candidates, not validated performance defaults.
- Reuse the existing mHC correctness suite. Add FP64 reference, cancellation/weight-reconstruction, output-boundary and changed-input/weight CUDA graph tests.
- Add a CUPTI benchmark that checks correctness before timing and sweeps both DeepGEMM and candidate configurations with CUDA graphs and cold L2. Weight preparation, allocations and the common epilogue are excluded from the reported prenorm timing.

The prepared weights occupy 6 bytes per original FP32 element, in addition to any retained original weight. The caller must rebuild them after weight updates. Different accumulation orders can change outputs; batch invariance is not promised. SGLang's bundled serving gains are not an estimate for this isolated kernel or for vLLM.

## Duplicate check and provenance

Checked #57448 and public open/closed PR searches for `mHC`, `compensated`, `bf16x3`, `SM90`, and Hopper on 2026-10-09. No open PR implementing this compensated mHC projection was found.

- #60768 only opts SM90 into the existing TF32 coefficient-overlap path; this is an independent kernel draft, not a duplicate or dependency.
- #57603 implements small-batch overlap; #56633 fuses post/pre; #56962 integrates Mega-mHC. They are relevant baselines, not this BF16x3 projection.
- #60376 is a router-GEMM optimization on SM100, not mHC prenorm on SM90.
- #59129 concerns the separate DeepGEMM SM90 correctness fix and must be accounted for when benchmarking the baseline.

The SGLang kernel's Apache-2.0 attribution is retained. Reviewed source: `python/sglang/kernels/ops/layernorm/mhc.py` on SGLang main around `5d8e98b7fdd83907616b1ff8ca68229f2ae95b34`. This adapts its numerical approach to vLLM's output layout and caller-owned workspace; it does not copy SGLang's runtime dispatch or Sinkhorn implementation.

## Validation completed

CPU-only Linux container, Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1. Source under test was overlaid into an isolated source checkout; dependencies came from the existing vLLM v0.28.0 image, not a newly built wheel. Container used `runc`, no GPU device nodes, empty `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void`, no network, 2 CPU cores and 4 GiB RAM. `torch.cuda.is_available()` was false.

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH=$PWD PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/kernels/mhc -o addopts= \
  -q tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_kernels.py -k bf16x3
```

**3 passed, 9 GPU cases skipped, 320 deselected.** CPU checks cover random, cancellation and scaled FP32 weight decomposition, including preserving the original weight. Source-only version/extension warnings and torch deprecation warnings were emitted.

**18 SM90 offline compilations passed:** explicit `GPUTarget("cuda", 90, 32)`, K=5120/20480, splits=1/4/16, BLOCK_M=32/64/128, N=24, BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=64, four warps and three stages. PTX/cubin were generated without loading or launching a CUDA kernel. This proves compilation only, not GPU numerical correctness or speed.

All applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including Ruff, mypy, SPDX and Buildkite test tethering; `git diff --check` passed. The existing mHC CI job exercises the suite on B200; actual SM90 execution remains a validation gap.

## Before ready for review

- [ ] Run the 9 CUDA correctness/replay cases on SM90, including bounds checking.
- [ ] Run `benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_mhc_bf16x3.py` on H20/H200 and retain all configurations, not only winners.
- [ ] Integrate opt-in dispatch with weight-update handling and startup warmup only if the kernel is competitive against the actual fused post/pre baseline.
- [ ] Compare the complete mHC boundary and full serving performance; evaluate model quality after integration.
- [ ] Complete human line-by-line review.

AI assistance: implemented and checked with OpenAI Codex. This draft was opened at the human author's explicit request to stage the implementation while GPU resources are being arranged. GPU execution, model evaluations, serving benchmarks and human review are pending; this is not ready to merge.

title: [Perf][Kernel] Tune fused mHC post + pre-norm for SM90 at up to 8 tokens
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

The fused mHC post + pre-norm kernel runs twice per decoder layer in DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 and GLM-5.3-Flash. Its split configs were tuned on GB300 (#56633). This PR gives SM90 its own config for 1–8 tokens: `(tile_n, n_splits, n_thr) = (12, hidden / 512, 256)`. Other architectures and token counts are unchanged.

## Claims

- On H20 at 1–8 tokens, the op gets faster:
  - DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash (hidden 4096): 4.4–16.3%.
  - DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (hidden 5120): 9.1–14.1%.
  - DeepSeek-V4-Pro (hidden 7168): 2.1–22.8%.
- The band includes DSpark k=5 decode at C1, which runs 6 tokens per step.
- Residual streams are bit-identical. The mixing coefficients, and through them the layer inputs, differ only in FP32 summation order.
- Startup warmup compiles the new variant. Off SM90, the set of compiled kernels is unchanged.

## Validation

**Microbenchmark.** H20, `hc_mult = 4`, FlashInfer CUPTI with a CUDA graph and a cold L2, median of 3 runs of 200 replays. Outputs are checked before timing.
- The 4096 and 7168 columns time `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`, which DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3-Flash call.
- The 5120 column times `mhc_fused_post_pre_delayed_tilelang`, which DeepSeek-V4.1 calls.

All columns come from one run of this PR's `tilelang_kernels.py`. Each cell is main → this PR, in µs.

| Tokens | 4096 | 5120 | 7168 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 10.94 → 10.05 (−8.2%) | 11.58 → 9.98 (−13.8%) | 13.92 → 10.75 (−22.8%) |
| 2 | 10.85 → 9.84 (−9.3%) | 11.55 → 10.08 (−12.8%) | 13.54 → 10.62 (−21.5%) |
| 3 | 11.04 → 10.14 (−8.1%) | 11.73 → 10.08 (−14.1%) | 13.70 → 11.30 (−17.5%) |
| 4 | 10.82 → 9.86 (−8.9%) | 11.62 → 10.14 (−12.7%) | 13.50 → 11.20 (−17.1%) |
| 5 | 10.85 → 9.82 (−9.4%) | 11.60 → 10.46 (−9.8%) | 13.63 → 11.30 (−17.1%) |
| 6 | 10.85 → 10.24 (−5.6%) | 11.65 → 10.59 (−9.1%) | 13.66 → 13.38 (−2.1%) |
| 7 | 11.01 → 10.53 (−4.4%) | 11.71 → 10.59 (−9.6%) | 13.86 → 13.54 (−2.3%) |
| 8 | 12.48 → 10.45 (−16.3%) | 13.54 → 11.68 (−13.7%) | 16.42 → 14.21 (−13.5%) |

- The minimum tensor traffic is 1.7–3.9 MB per op, corresponding to an effective bandwidth of 152–308 GB/s.
- From 9 to 32 tokens, main and this PR pick the same config, and their times agree within ±1.1%.
- At 5120, the new config had the lowest total time over 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 tokens in a sweep of 63 configs. It was within 4.6% of the best config at each of those token counts.

**Tests.** `pytest tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_jit_warmup.py tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_kernels.py` passes on H20, with one exception: `test_mhc_fused_post_pre[4-7168-128]`. That case runs 128 tokens, outside the band, and fails the same way without this change.

A 1-hour TP8 serving run built no TileLang kernels after warmup. CI runs `kernels/mhc` on B200 only, so this H20 run is the only coverage for the SM90 cases.

**E2E sanity check.** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 8×H20 with TP8, 1K in / 1K out. It ran on main 240ee8d (2026-10-07) with this change applied; `kernels/mhc/` has not changed since.
- DSpark k=5 at a synthetic acceptance length of 3.51.
- One run per server, in the order main, PR, PR, main.

At C1, both PR runs beat both main runs: output throughput +0.9%, TPOT p50 −1.0%. At C64, which is outside the band, both PR runs fall between main's two runs in throughput and TPOT p50.

**Accuracy.** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on the same build, GSM8K, 5-shot, with real DSpark verification:
- Correct answers: 1274 / 1319 on main, 1276 / 1319 with this PR.
- Acceptance length: 3.863 and 3.868.

GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4 were checked at the op level only.

## Details

- **Why it is faster.** Every (token, tile, k-slice) block recomputes the post mapping.
  - main's `(2, 8, 128)` runs 12 tiles, and each thread makes 4–7 serial memory round trips.
  - The new config runs 2 tiles with 2 round trips each.

- **H100/H200.** These GPUs are not measured. Both grids should fit in one wave on 132 SMs, so the gain is expected to carry over. The 6–7-token dip at 7168 looks like a wave spill on H20 and is not expected there.
- **Scope.** SM100, SM120 and ROCm are untouched. No open PR changes this config.

title: [Bugfix] Package the SM90 DeepGEMM mHC register lifetime fix
body:
## Purpose

Package the SM90 mHC prenorm GEMM register-lifetime fix from [deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#448](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/448), authored by jason (leevan). In a multi-stage K loop, the next iteration can overwrite register A operands before the previous asynchronous WGMMA has finished. Repeated calls with identical inputs can therefore produce different outputs. The upstream fix waits immediately after committing the WGMMA batch.

This integrates that existing fix into vLLM's packaged JIT header until the pinned DeepGEMM dependency contains it; it is not a new kernel implementation. DeepGEMM #448 is currently open. Remove the temporary integration once the dependency pin includes the fix.

This correctness change was split out of [vLLM #58986](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58986), which now contains only the H20 block-FP8 MoE tuning. This branch starts from main `07f1ba2ec66776650a490630ddfa9e3c92713c33` and does not depend on that performance PR. The corresponding v0.30 backport remains [mengziheng/vllm#3](https://github.com/mengziheng/vllm/pull/3). There is no throughput improvement claim for this correctness repair.

## Changes

- Generate a patched header during CMake configuration and install it without modifying a supplied `DEEPGEMM_SRC_DIR`. Exclude the original header from the directory install to prevent a same-timestamp overwrite.
- Use the same helper in the standalone DeepGEMM installer. Recognized patched input is idempotent; unrecognized source fails without overwriting the destination.
- Extend the existing mHC suite with six SM90 regressions: 256/512/1024 tokens, different split-K counts, default and side streams, independent FP32 references and exact repeatability. Skip when DeepGEMM is unavailable.

## Validation

The following GPU results were recorded on H20/v0.30 before this PR split. The main test path is `tests/kernels/mhc/test_mhc_kernels.py`; the v0.30 suite used `tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py`.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py \
  -k 'sm90_mhc_prenorm_preserves_register_operands or test_mhc_fused_post_pre' -v
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py \
  -k sm90_mhc_prenorm_preserves_register_operands -v
```

- The pinned original header fails the new regression; the fixed header passes all six cases. The final test including its DeepGEMM availability guard returned **6 passed, 212 deselected**.

title: [Spec Decode] Enable adaptive verification on DSv4 + sm90
body:
## Purpose

Enable adaptive verification for the DeepSeek V4 indexer on Hopper (SM90).

The native variable-length DeepGEMM paged-MQA path remains restricted to SM100. On SM90, this change instead uses the existing flattened decode path and builds the single-token rows from the device-side decode lengths. This is necessary because adaptive verification can trim each request to a different length while the CPU metadata contains only a uniform placeholder. The builder forces this device-length flattening for adaptive verification, advertises support for the device/CPU query-length mismatch, and enables CUDA graph capture for this path. When there is only one decode request, the CPU and device request boundaries necessarily agree, so that case reuses the cheaper uniform flattened metadata path.

This addresses the Hopper startup failure reported in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47808#issuecomment-5264762911.

### Duplicate-work check

I searched the open PRs for `adaptive verification Hopper SM90`, `DeepseekV4IndexerBackend adaptive verification`, `varlen indexer Hopper`, and `SM90 DeepGEMM indexer`; no open PR implements this fix. #51972 concerns a separate indexer bounds bug, while #47808 is the merged SM100 implementation where the SM90 failure was reported.

## Test Plan

Targeted correctness and regression tests:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_native_next_n.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py -v
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_batch_ordering.py -v
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_deepgemm_attention.py -v
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD
```

End-to-end validation used DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on 4x H200 (SM90):

- TP2 / DP2 / expert parallel startup and serving with 7 DSpark speculative tokens, probabilistic drafting, and adaptive verification enabled.
- The repository GSM8K 5-shot evaluation with TP4 / expert parallel and the adaptive DSpark configuration from `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark-confidence-TP4.yaml`. The Blackwell-only `--attention_config.indexer_kv_dtype=mxfp4` option was removed for Hopper; the rest of the speculative configuration was unchanged.
- Warmed throughput comparison against fixed verification on TP2 / DP2 / expert parallel, averaged over three runs.
- Matched fixed and adaptive torch-profiler traces at concurrency one.

## Test Result

- Indexer and adaptive-verification tests: **15 passed**.
- GPU batch-ordering tests: **10 passed**.
- DeepGEMM attention kernel tests on H200: **5 passed**.
- Pre-commit, including ruff and Python 3.10 mypy: **passed**.
- User-equivalent 4x H200 server: **started and served successfully**. The log confirms `use_flattening=True supports_varlen=False`.
- Hopper GSM8K: **94.996% accuracy**, **0% invalid**, **4.106 mean acceptance length** (1,319 questions, 5-shot).

Warmed output throughput (tokens/s):

| Concurrency | Fixed verification | Adaptive verification | Delta |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 256.5 | 240.2 | -6.35% |
| 16 | 1520.9 | 1608.9 | +5.78% |
| 64 | 2663.6 | 3032.5 | +13.85% |

The concurrency-one regression is reduced but remains a known limitation of this draft. Reusing uniform flattened metadata for a single decode request improved adaptive throughput from 236.9 to 240.2 tokens/s (+1.4%) and reduced mean ITL from 12.455 to 12.355 ms. This matches the metadata microbenchmark: device-ragged preparation took 115.08 us versus 24.14 us for uniform preparation, accounting for about 0.100 ms of the original 0.961 ms per-verification-step gap.

Matched torch-profiler traces show that fixed and adaptive verification both execute an 8-token target graph at concurrency one. Median target GPU execution was effectively identical (10.181 ms fixed versus 10.185 ms adaptive), but the median gap between target graph executions increased from 1.811 to 2.517 ms. The adaptive trace contains one blocking confidence-copy event synchronization per step in `AdaptiveVerificationManager.record_confidences`; its approximately 0.706 ms net critical-path effect, together with the 0.100 ms metadata cost, explains most of the original step-latency gap. CUDA graph capture also increased in the TP2 / DP2 comparison (121 s / 4.71 GiB adaptive versus 52 s / 2.61 GiB fixed). The existing SM100 path is unchanged and was not rebenchmarked here.

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Cap DFlash/DSpark profiling query batch
body:
Fixes #56443.

## Root Cause
The memory-profiling dummy run can hand-build max_num_seqs requests without applying the scheduler's speculative query-token budget. For DSpark/DFlash, each request can require num_query_per_req draft query rows.
For example, with max_num_seqs=512, max_num_batched_tokens=2048, and DSpark K=5, the profiling path asks the speculator for 512 * 5 = 2560 query rows while its input buffers are sized for 2048 rows, so DSpark can read _anchor_idx past input_ids and later surface CUDA IndexKernel/device-side assert errors.

## Changes
Cap the initial dummy/profile draft-generation pass to the largest complete set of query blocks that fits the speculator input buffer, preserve the full target-context and sampler projection for memory profiling, and fail early with a clear ValueError if a real query batch exceeds the input buffer.

Other profiling dummy runs, including FlashInfer autotune, build target attention metadata and cannot use the initial skip-attention shortcut. Add a default no-op speculator hook that lets DFlash-family speculators cap the dummy request count before GPUModelRunner builds those synthetic batches. This does not affect real serving requests or other speculator implementations.

## Existing PRs

#53970 addresses the same `max_num_seqs * parallel-draft query width > max_num_batched_tokens` failure condition with a broader capacity-based fix: it raises `max_num_batched_tokens` to cover the worst-case parallel-draft batch and enlarges the DFlash input buffers. This PR instead leaves the configured target token budget unchanged and caps only synthetic profiling batches to the existing speculator capacity. It covers both the initial skip-attention memory profile and full-attention profiling dummy runs such as FlashInfer autotune, and adds a fail-fast check if a real serving batch violates the scheduler invariant already established by #51256. The approaches are alternatives for the startup crash, but differ in scope and memory/scheduling impact.

#53080 separates target and draft scheduler budgets, but it does not constrain model-runner-generated profiling batches that bypass normal scheduler admission. #53577 covers broader DSpark/PP and padded graph safety work, but it has no matching profile query-buffer cap. #55133 and #56387 address different DSpark failure modes.

title: [Model][Quant] DeepSeek-V4: opt-in lossless MXFP4->block-FP8 expert dequant (Hopper prefill speedup)
body:
# [Model][Quant] DeepSeek-V4: opt-in lossless MXFP4→block-FP8 expert dequant (Hopper prefill speedup)

## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4 Instruct checkpoints (e.g. `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`) ship MXFP4
routed experts. On Hopper (SM90) vLLM runs these through the Marlin W4A16 MoE
kernel. This adds an opt-in path (`VLLM_DSV4_FP4_DEQUANT=1`) that losslessly
re-encodes the MXFP4 experts to block-FP8 (e4m3, 128×128 scales) at load time
and runs them through the existing block-FP8 MoE kernel (FP8 tensor cores),
giving materially higher prefill throughput on Hopper. The trade-off is larger
expert weight memory (FP8 is 2× MXFP4), so it is strictly opt-in; MXFP4/Marlin
remains the default.

The re-encode is **bit-exact**: MX scales are pure powers of two (e8m0) and
e4m3 has enough mantissa/range to absorb the per-32-group scale ratio into the
stored value (`max_fp4 6.0 × 2^6 = 384 < 448`), so no precision is lost relative
to the MXFP4 weights.

### Why Hopper specifically

The native MXFP4 W4A8/W4-MXFP8 MoE backends (`DEEPGEMM_MXFP4`,
`FLASHINFER_TRTLLM_MXFP4_MXFP8`, `FLASHINFER_CUTLASS_MXFP4_MXFP8`) keep 4-bit
weight storage *and* use FP8 tensor cores, but their `is_supported_config`
gates them to Blackwell (`is_device_capability_family(100)`/`(120)`). On SM90
only Marlin W4A16 passes, so Hopper has no FP8-tensor-core MoE path for these
checkpoints today. A native SM90 W4AFP8 grouped MoE is still an open request
(vllm-project/vllm#49977). This opt-in dequant→FP8 gives Hopper that fast path
now; the cost is 2× expert weight memory (FP8 vs MXFP4). A true SM90 W4A8
kernel would supersede it by keeping 4-bit storage — left as follow-up.

## Not a duplicate

Searched open PRs/issues (`mxfp4 fp8 dequant experts`, `DeepSeek-V4 fp4 fp8`,
`deepseek_v4 hopper`, `fp8 experts hopper block`). Existing DeepSeek-V4 work is
orthogonal: W4A4 MegaMoE (#42844, Blackwell), SM12x/ROCm enablement (#41834,
#41601), indexer caches (#48505, #49085, #51209), e8m0 loader bugfix (#51946).
None provides a Hopper MXFP4→FP8 expert fast path.

## Changes

- `vllm/envs.py`: register `VLLM_DSV4_FP4_DEQUANT` (default off).
- `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/fp4_dequant.py`: `cast_mxfp4_to_fp8_block` (lossless
  re-encode) + `DsV4Fp4DequantMoEMethod(Fp8MoEMethod)` (loads MXFP4 via
  `Mxfp4MoEMethod.create_weights`, converts in `process_weights_after_loading`,
  reuses the block-FP8 kernel/apply).
- `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/quant_config.py`: route fp4 experts to the dequant
  method when the flag is set.
- `tests/quantization/test_dsv4_fp4_dequant.py`: bit-exactness + dim-guard tests.

## Tests

- Unit: `pytest tests/quantization/test_dsv4_fp4_dequant.py` → **5 passed**
  (H20 box, torch 2.11/cu130) — bit-exact re-encode across shapes (256×256,
  256×512, 512×256, 128×1024) + rejects unaligned dims.
- Lint: `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` (v0.14.0, pinned in
  `.pre-commit-config.yaml`) clean on all changed files.
- Serving smoke (H20, TP=4, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, `VLLM_DSV4_FP4_DEQUANT=1`):
  loads, `fp8_w8a8` block[128,128] MoE active, CUDA graph OK, correct outputs.

## Model evaluation

- End-to-end prefill (single request, TTFT, unique prompts, TP=4, H20):
  | input len | Marlin W4A16 (default) | this PR (dequant→FP8) | speedup |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 2048 | 7020 tok/s | 10752 tok/s | 1.53× |
  | 4096 | 8129 tok/s | 11882 tok/s | 1.46× |
  | 8192 | 8396 tok/s | 11623 tok/s | 1.38× |
